entries.clue: Unconventional romance for old premier (7)

indicatorNotes.Unconventional: Something unconventional refuses the usual arrangement, so the letters beside it will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: seven letters to be reordered

annotation.surface: An unusual love affair involving a former head of government.
annotation.walkthrough: David Cameron led the UK government from 2010 to 2016, so 'old premier' is recent history rather than anything ancient. One word of the clue carries the whole of the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A premier is a prime minister, and Cameron held that office in Britain until 2016, which makes him an old one.

entries.clue: Inspector, one from Baltic area formerly, opposed to triflers (10)

blocks.note: DI is a detective inspector, the rank British police forces abbreviate that way
a Lett is a Latvian, the older English name for a native of that Baltic state
anti is the preposition meaning against

annotation.surface: A police officer of Baltic extraction taking a stand against people who do not take things seriously.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Inspector' hides the join: the rank and the nationality are two separate chunks of letters, not one man's description. 'Formerly' is the flag on the nationality, because Lett has long since given way to Latvian.
annotation.definitionFit: Dilettanti dabble at an art without ever going deep, so they trifle with it, and the Italian plural matches the plural definition.

entries.clue: Grim leap on and off for lizard (4)

indicatorNotes.on and off: Something done on and off happens every other time, so letters are picked out every other one.

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of these two words, read in order

annotation.surface: A bleak jump attempted only now and then.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words have to be read as one run of eight letters with the space ignored, which is what makes the alternation hard to spot. The Gila monster takes its name from the Gila river in Arizona.
annotation.definitionFit: The Gila monster is the venomous lizard of the American southwest, and setters clue it by the first word of its name on its own.

entries.clue: Latitude following English actor given award (7)

blocks.note: f. is the reference-book abbreviation for following, as in 'page 20f.'
Oliver Reed, the English film actor
the Order of Merit, a British honour in the monarch's personal gift

annotation.surface: An English actor being handed a prize.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like a positional instruction saying what goes after what; it is the single letter footnotes use. Oliver Reed was one of British cinema's best-known hellraisers, and the Order of Merit is limited to twenty-four living holders.
annotation.definitionFit: Latitude is room to act as you choose — the sense in 'giving someone latitude' — so one abstract noun stands for the other.

entries.clue: Base for shuttles? (6,4)

blocks.note: read as a depot or headquarters, the yard a service works out of, and meant as the patch of prepared ground a rocket leaves from
read as the little buses and trains that run back and forth all day, and meant as the reusable spacecraft NASA flew

annotation.surface: The depot a shuttle bus service operates out of.
annotation.walkthrough: Shuttle buses and shuttle trains are what the word usually means, and a base for those is a garage. The question mark warns that the other shuttle is wanted — the spacecraft NASA flew from Cape Canaveral until 2011.
annotation.definitionFit: A launch site is the prepared ground a spacecraft lifts off from, which is the one sense in which a space shuttle can be said to have a base.

entries.clue: Lack of wind in local mountains (4)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in something sits inside it, so the letters are to be found unbroken within the words that follow.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters spanning the gap between the two words

annotation.surface: Still air among the hills nearby.
annotation.walkthrough: Hidden words like to straddle a word break, and this one takes three letters from the end of one word and one from the start of the next. 'Local' earns its place in the picture and is there only for the letters it lends.
annotation.definitionFit: A calm is a spell of windless weather — the sailor's flat calm — so the noun answers the noun phrase directly.

entries.clue: Mum has to set aside small vegetable (7)

blocks.note: to keep mum is to keep quiet, and sh is the noise that asks for quiet
to allot something is to set it aside for a particular purpose

annotation.surface: A mother having to put a small vegetable by.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mum' is the silence word, not the parent, and the clue's picture depends on you taking the parent. The definition needs both its words: a shallot is not any vegetable but a small clustered onion.
annotation.definitionFit: A shallot is a small mild onion grown in clumps, so the size in the definition is doing real work rather than padding.

entries.clue: Casual household (8)

blocks.note: the unbuttoned sense: being on easy, informal terms with someone
the sense in 'a household name', meaning known to absolutely everybody

annotation.surface: A home where nobody stands on ceremony.
annotation.walkthrough: Two adjectives butted together with nothing joining them, which is why an eight-letter answer arrives dressed as a two-word phrase. 'Household' is the harder half, and it wants the adjective rather than the noun.
annotation.definitionFit: Familiar covers both: a familiar manner is a casual one, and a familiar name is a household name.

entries.clue: Dislike trio of characters leaving for lack of enthusiasm (6)

indicatorNotes.leaving: What leaves goes away, so the letters named just before it are taken out of the word they sit in.

blocks.note: antipathy is a settled dislike of something
three letters standing together behind the opening one; the clue does not say which three, and only this trio leaves a word behind

annotation.surface: Someone's dislike fading as three people walk out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Characters' means letters here, not people, and the surface works hard to sell you actors or figures leaving a room. Strip three from a word for strong dislike and a far weaker feeling is what remains.
annotation.definitionFit: Apathy is the state of not caring enough to act on anything, which is exactly what a lack of enthusiasm amounts to.

entries.clue: Produce green bananas at back of store (8)

indicatorNotes.bananas: To go bananas is to go out of your mind, and letters out of their minds will not line up in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.back of: The back of a word is the letter it finishes on, so only that last one is taken.

blocks.note: five letters reordered
the clue's own little word, spelling itself out
the letter this word finishes on

annotation.surface: Unripe fruit stacked at the rear of a shop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At' is the sly one: it looks like nothing but a preposition placing the fruit in the shop, and it hands over two of the eight letters untouched. The definition wants the verb, while the greengrocer's noun is what the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: To generate something is to produce it — power, heat, interest — and both are transitive verbs in the same form.

entries.clue: Fancy meal in US city to be specific (6)

indicatorNotes.Fancy: 'Fancy' here is the verb meaning imagine, and what you are asked to imagine is the letters standing in some other order.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' names the destination: what comes before it is buried inside what comes after.

blocks.note: NY is New York, the short form on every address label
four letters reordered before they go inside

annotation.surface: An elaborate dinner eaten in an American city.
annotation.walkthrough: The city is the two-letter one every crossword leans on, so the four letters of the dinner have nowhere to go except between them. The definition is a whole phrase, which is why no single word of the clue looks like one.
annotation.definitionFit: Namely introduces the particular thing you mean — 'one guest, namely her brother' — so it does the job of 'to be specific' in a sentence.

entries.clue: Detest photo created behind cricketer still showing fear? (6,2,3,4)

indicatorNotes.created: What is created is made new out of the material to hand, so those letters come out in a new arrangement.
indicatorNotes.behind: Behind means round the back, so the letters it governs are written after the piece named next rather than before it.

blocks.note: Joe Root, England's Test batsman and former captain
eleven letters reordered

annotation.surface: A loathed photograph taken behind a cricketer who has gone rigid with fright.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cricketer' is a surname, not a role: Joe Root has captained England at Test cricket for years. Eleven of the fifteen letters come out of the clue's first two words, which is why so long an answer has so short a clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone rooted to the spot cannot move a muscle, and fear is the usual thing that does it, so the phrase says standing stock still in fright.

entries.clue: First person’s held up in this deal arranged for chef (5,5)

indicatorNotes.held up: In a down entry what is held up is written upwards, so its letters read from the bottom of the grid towards the top.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' puts what comes before it inside what comes after.
indicatorNotes.arranged: Things that have been arranged have been put into somebody's chosen order, not the one they arrived in.

blocks.note: eight letters reordered, with a gap left for the pair below
the first person speaking says I'm, and those two letters go up the grid rather than down

annotation.surface: A deal being put together for a cook, with the speaker's own share held back inside it.
annotation.walkthrough: The first person in a crossword is I or I'm, and here it is the contraction, turned round because the entry runs downwards. Delia Smith taught Britain to cook through BBC series and books from the 1970s on.
annotation.definitionFit: Delia Smith is the television cook whose recipe books have sold millions of copies in Britain, so 'chef' names her by her trade.

entries.clue: State about to feature in a UK shoot for broadcast (5,5)

indicatorNotes.to feature in: To feature in something is to appear inside it, so this pair of letters goes within the letters named next.
indicatorNotes.for broadcast: To broadcast seed is to scatter it far and wide, and scattered letters land in an order of their own.

blocks.note: eight letters reordered, with room left inside for the pair below
re is the memo-heading word for about, as in 'Re: your letter'

annotation.surface: A country almost appearing in a British film shoot destined for television.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is a scattering word here, not a sound word — nothing in this clue is said aloud, and the farming sense of sowing seed is where the crossword usage comes from. 'Shoot' belongs to the film crew in the picture and to the letter heap in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: South Korea is a sovereign country, and 'state' is the ordinary word for one, so the definition is as plain as it looks.

entries.clue: View complication with no end of disgust (5)

indicatorNotes.with no: 'No' in front of a thing is an instruction to do without it, so whatever it names is struck out.
indicatorNotes.end of: The end of a word is the letter it finishes on, so only that one is taken.

blocks.note: a tangle is a complication, a knot of trouble
the letter this word finishes on, and the one that has to go

annotation.surface: Looking at a mess with limitless revulsion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'No end of disgust' means plenty of it in ordinary English, and that reading has to be thrown away: the clue wants 'no' plus 'end of disgust', which is a single letter. That letter turns out to be the front of the word it comes off.
annotation.definitionFit: An angle is the view you take of something — the angle you come at a story from — so the noun stands in for a point of view.

entries.clue: Sign jazz musician is wanting grand (5)

indicatorNotes.wanting: Something wanting is something lacking, so the letter named next is missing from the word it belongs to.

blocks.note: Charles Mingus, the American bassist and bandleader
a grand is a thousand pounds, abbreviated to its first letter

annotation.surface: A jazz player who is short of a thousand pounds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grand' sits right beside a musician, so a piano is what you picture; the money sense is wanted, and it is worth one letter. Charles Mingus led his own bands through the 1950s and 60s.
annotation.definitionFit: The minus sign is the bar written between two numbers to take one from the other, so 'sign' names it by what it is.

entries.clue: Asian bread in a fine country snubbed by India (7)

indicatorNotes.snubbed: To snub someone is to cut them short, and a word cut short loses the letter it ends on.

blocks.note: the article, taken as it stands
F is the grade stamped on a fine pencil lead
Ghana, the West African republic, docked of its final letter
I is India in the radio alphabet

annotation.surface: A flatbread from Asia sold in a pleasant country that India has cold-shouldered.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is money and not baking, which is what makes the Asian flatbread in the surface such a good decoy. 'India' is the radio alphabet's letter rather than the nation, so the clue points east twice and means something else both times.
annotation.definitionFit: Bread is slang for money, and the afghani is the unit Afghanistan pays in, which places it squarely in Asia.

entries.clue: Hate dish endlessly covered by exotic seeds (7)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: Endlessly means without an end, so the word gives up the letter it finishes on.
indicatorNotes.covered by: What covers a thing lies over it on either side, so the letters named after this close round the ones named before.
indicatorNotes.exotic: Exotic means foreign and strange-looking, and letters made strange are letters set down in an unfamiliar order.

blocks.note: five letters reordered so they can wrap round the pair below
a pie is a dish, and taking its end off leaves two letters

annotation.surface: A dish smothered under a scattering of unusual seeds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' is a signal for a lost last letter, not a remark about how long the meal went on. 'Hate' at the front is the definition, though it reads as the diner's opinion of what is on the plate.
annotation.definitionFit: To despise something is to look down on it with contempt, which is hate with a sneer in it, and both are verbs in the same form.

entries.clue: Popular advertising with pointer in the East End describing a good book? (2,5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a description rather than a synonym: it says what state a book is in instead of naming a thing, which is why it opens with a participle.

indicatorNotes.in the East End: The East End is working-class London, where the local accent drops the aitch off the front of a word.

blocks.note: in means fashionable — the in crowd, the in thing
PR is public relations, the trade that publicises a client
a pointer is a hint, and the accent named next takes its aitch away

annotation.surface: A well-liked ad campaign with a tip from east London about a worthwhile read.
annotation.walkthrough: The Good Book is the Bible, which is what the lower-case 'a good book' is quietly teasing. Nothing here is said aloud: the dropped aitch is a deletion in the spelling, and the rest is three chunks laid end to end.
annotation.definitionFit: A book in print is one its publisher still has available to sell, so the phrase describes the book's state rather than naming any book.

entries.clue: Plane then flying east of continent is type of jumbo (7,8)

indicatorNotes.flying: Letters in flight are off the ground and out of their given order, so they come down in another one.
indicatorNotes.east of: On an across entry east is to the right, so whatever is east of a piece is written after it.

blocks.note: the second largest of the continents
nine letters reordered

annotation.surface: An aircraft heading east past a landmass, described as a kind of jumbo jet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jumbo' is a jet in the surface and an animal in the answer: Jumbo was a real elephant at London Zoo, sold to Barnum in 1882, and the aeroplane borrowed his name. 'Plane' is fodder, not a second aircraft.
annotation.definitionFit: Jumbo, the Victorian circus elephant the jet was named after, was an African one, so 'type of jumbo' is asking which species he belonged to.

entries.clue: Evidence of cold hospital put in place by English and US company (6)

indicatorNotes.put in: To put one thing in another is to set it inside, so the letter named before this goes between the letters named after.

blocks.note: Pl. is how a street name ending in Place is shortened on a map
H is the letter on the British road sign pointing to a hospital
E is the standard short form for English
General Motors, the Detroit carmaker

annotation.surface: A chilly hospital built by an English firm together with an American one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cold' belongs to the definition and not to the hospital beside it, and that join without a comma is the whole disguise. GM is General Motors, the Detroit company behind Chevrolet and Cadillac.
annotation.definitionFit: Phlegm is the thick mucus a head cold brings up, so producing it is the plainest evidence that someone has one.

entries.clue: Detectives entering Surrey estate (4)

indicatorNotes.entering: What enters a place is inside it, so the letters sit unbroken within the words that follow.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters bridging the two words

annotation.surface: Plain-clothes officers arriving at a property in Surrey.
annotation.walkthrough: Private eyes are detectives, which is the sense that lets a four-letter plural define a plainclothes plural. Surrey is the county immediately south-west of London, and its name is here purely for the letters it lends.
annotation.definitionFit: A private eye is a private detective, and the shortened form carries the same meaning in the plural.

entries.clue: Rex probes risky rooms for guests (8)

indicatorNotes.probes: To probe something is to push into it, so the letter named before this word goes inside the word named after.

blocks.note: parlous is an old word for perilous, surviving in the phrase 'a parlous state'
R is rex, Latin for king, the R in a monarch's signature

annotation.surface: A king poking about in some dangerous guest rooms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rex' reads as somebody's name and is the Latin one on coins and postboxes. Parlous and perilous are the same word worn down two different ways, which is why one of them sounds archaic.
annotation.definitionFit: A parlour is the front room a household keeps for receiving visitors, so the plural is precisely rooms for guests.

entries.clue: Reportedly, study part for a clarinet (4)

indicatorNotes.Reportedly: What is reported is spoken, so what is wanted is a word that sounds the same and is spelt differently.

blocks.note: to study a subject is to read it, and that verb in the present tense is said the same way but written otherwise

annotation.surface: A report that someone is studying part of a clarinet.
annotation.walkthrough: Everything turns on the two pronunciations of one spelling: 'study' points at the present tense of the verb, which is said the way the grid wants it written. The thing itself is the thin cane blade clamped in a clarinet's mouthpiece.
annotation.definitionFit: The reed is the sliver of cane in a clarinet's mouthpiece that vibrates to make the note, so it is a component made for that instrument.

entries.clue: Find uncovered opening for coin (6)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: A cover is what sits on the outside, so uncovering a word strips its first and last letters and leaves the middle.

blocks.note: the two letters left in the middle once the outer ones come off
a vent is an opening cut to let air through

annotation.surface: Coming across an uncovered slot that takes a coin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coin' is the verb, as in coining a phrase, and not the thing that goes into a slot. 'Find' misleads the same way: it is a word to be stripped, not an instruction to look for anything.
annotation.definitionFit: To coin a word or a phrase is to invent it, so one verb replaces the other; the money sense is the setter's decoy.

entries.clue: Four points to keep plant in unlicensed establishments (8)

indicatorNotes.to keep: To keep something is to hold on to it, so the letters named before close round whatever follows.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' says where the plant goes: inside the letters already set down.

blocks.note: south, east, north and south — four compass letters, one of them used twice
a hebe is a small evergreen shrub with spikes of flowers, common in British gardens

annotation.surface: A plant being kept between four points of the compass on premises with no licence.
annotation.walkthrough: The four points are not four different ones — one compass letter is used twice, which is why the outside is longer than the bearings suggest. A shebeen was originally an Irish drinking den without a licence, and the word travelled to South Africa.
annotation.definitionFit: A shebeen sells drink with no licence to do so, so the plural names exactly that sort of premises.
